RT: @MalwareTechBlog I'll be the first to admit I'm mediocre at exploit development, but I am in contact with enough extremely talented exploit developers to say this for certain:

Anyone claiming they were "easily" able to generate a working php2shell exploit with AI is either:

a) a world-class exploit developer with an extreme case of imposter syndrome.

b) currently looking at some very confident-sounding but wrong LLM output.

I'm rather certain it's the latter based on the number of AI-hallucinated exploits I've seen posted on GitHub. Threat actors are also blasting my honeypot network with "php2shell" exploits that not only don't work, but aren't even within 10,000 miles of anything to do with how the exploit actually works.

I've seen the same technique from the attached image in multiple alleged "php2shell exploits", including one on GitHub with over 100 stars. Problem is, it's not php2shell, nor is it even a vulnerability at all. It's a technique known as "session poisoning", which can be leveraged to exploit local file inclusion (LFI) vulnerabilities in PHP apps (not PHP itself).

The only thing it has in common with CVE-2026-109618/CVE-2026-109619 is they both use the "PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" feature. And mitigation advice for both issues reference setting "session.upload_progress.enabled" to "Off".

People are shoving loose details of the vulnerability into LLMs, the LLMs are keying in on the "PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" string, then generating session poisoning code that has nothing to do with the actual CVE. And because the people doing this have absolutely no idea what they're doing, they're confident enough to post their "proof of concept exploit" to GitHub and share it on social media.

So if you see people talking about "session poisoning + LFI" it's likely their LLM hallucinated an exploit based on a 2018 blog by Orange Tsai talking about a local file inclusion attack vector.

What's even worse is that "security researchers" are then using LLMs to triage these exploitation attempts, falling victim to the same hallucinations, then confirming there is ongoing mass-exploitation (there currently isn't).

The actual real exploit is very difficult to exploit, and so far I've not seen anyone successfully get it working on more than a handful of PHP version with highly-specific configurations.

LLMs are useful tools in the hands of skilled professionals, but for others, they're often just a Dunning-Kruger accelerator.

PHP2Shell is two CVEs in the PHP runtime (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) that can lead to unauthenticated RCE.

When something like this lands, the first question is usually: what exactly is affected, and what do I need to patch?

I’d rather answer that from the terminal than from twelve browser tabs.

With the ZEN SecDB CLI:

1️⃣ secdb search php2shell

finds both CVEs.

2️⃣ secdb cve CVE-2026-109618

gives the full record: description, CVSS 4.0 at 9.2, CVSS 3.1 at 9.8, vectors, references and vendor advisories from Debian, Red Hat, SUSE, Ubuntu, Arch, Gentoo, FreeBSD and others.

That’s useful because you can quickly check whether your distro already ships a fix, instead of going through each security tracker manually.

If you run PHP, upgrade to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or use the patched package provided by your distro.

Configuration mitigations may reduce the risk, but they don’t replace patching.

🚨 This time the bug isn’t in your code, it’s in PHP itself.

PHP2Shell is two CVEs in the PHP runtime (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) that can lead to unauthenticated RCE.

When something like this lands, the first question is usually: what exactly is affected, and what do I need to patch?

I’d rather answer that from the terminal than from twelve browser tabs.

With the ZEN SecDB CLI:

1️⃣ secdb search php2shell

finds both CVEs.

2️⃣ secdb cve CVE-2026-109618

gives the full record: description, CVSS 4.0 at 9.2, CVSS 3.1 at 9.8, vectors, references and vendor advisories from Debian, Red Hat, SUSE, Ubuntu, Arch, Gentoo, FreeBSD and others.

That’s useful because you can quickly check whether your distro already ships a fix, instead of going through each security tracker manually.

If you run PHP, upgrade to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or use the patched package provided by your distro.

Configuration mitigations may reduce the risk, but they don’t replace patching.

And if the server was exposed, it’s probably worth checking whether it was already compromised.

PHP2Shell field report — the attacker-side view.

The first exploit-shaped request hit our Mirage honeypot fleet at 21:57 UTC on 20 Oct, ~16h before the patch embargo lifted. Over the next 48h: 9 source IPs, 7 countries, 2 distinct attack shapes.

Highlights:

One actor swept body size <1KB → 16KB+, 200+ unique payloads in 2 min — live calibration of the OOM trigger
The lead tool stamps ----p2shell<hex> into its multipart boundary: a zero-false-positive detection tell we haven’t seen documented elsewhere
A B8RAT/1.0 actor reaching for the deserialization path (CVE-2026-109619) while others hammer the OOM path (CVE-2026-109618)

posts.content: CVE-2026-89139: Temporal Worker Service lets any authenticated caller with a single-namespace write role run arbitrary commands via the subprocess compute provider. CVSS 9.9. No patch yet. Audit access and restrict writes. #CVE #infosec #cybersecurity https://www.valtersit.com/cve/CVE-2026-89139/

CVE-2026-89139.description: Temporal Server compiles a Worker Controller Instance module into its Worker Service, and that module registers a compute provider named subprocess whose function is to launch a worker by running a command on the machine hosting the Worker Service. The program name and the argument vector that provider executes are taken from the compute provider configuration supplied in the caller's request rather than from operator configuration. An authenticated caller holding only a write role in a single namespace can therefore configure a worker deployment version so that the Worker Service executes a command of the caller's choosing on its own host, under the account the server process runs as. Execution is immediate rather than deferred: the configuration handler invokes every provider using the invoke strategy directly after validating the submitted specification, so no scaling decision, task arrival, or unusual request sequence is required. Because the Worker Service process holds the persistence credentials for every namespace in the cluster and the cluster's TLS material, the consequence reaches beyond the caller's namespace to the cluster as a whole. The provider is present in the official temporal-server binaries and container images for the affected releases. The only control that can keep it unreachable is the compute provider allowlist, the per-namespace dynamic configuration setting workercontroller.compute_providers.enabled, and that control does not deny by default: its default value is an unset list, and the allowlist check is skipped entirely when the value is unset, so every registered compute provider is permitted, this one included. To determine whether a deployment is affected, check the following together. The deployed Temporal Server version is 1.31.0 or later and earlier than 1.31.3. The Worker Service is running, which it is in the default service set and therefore in a stock deployment. The effective per-namespace value of workercontroller.compute_providers.enabled is either unset or contains subprocess. And authorization is configured, meaning a real authorizer and claim mapper are in place; a deployment running with no authorizer already grants every caller unrestricted access to every namespace, so it has no namespace boundary for this to cross. Note that the separate per-namespace dynamic configuration setting workercontroller.enabled does not gate the affected path. It defaults to false, and a deployment that has never set it in any namespace is still affected, which was confirmed by running an affected release with no value for that setting present anywhere in dynamic configuration. To look for a compute configuration that is already attached, call DescribeWorkerDeploymentVersion for each worker deployment version in each namespace and check whether any scaling group's compute provider type is subprocess.

RT: @MalwareTechBlog I'll be the first to admit I'm mediocre at exploit development, but I am in contact with enough extremely talented exploit developers to say this for certain:

Anyone claiming they were "easily" able to generate a working php2shell exploit with AI is either:

a) a world-class exploit developer with an extreme case of imposter syndrome.

b) currently looking at some very confident-sounding but wrong LLM output.

I'm rather certain it's the latter based on the number of AI-hallucinated exploits I've seen posted on GitHub. Threat actors are also blasting my honeypot network with "php2shell" exploits that not only don't work, but aren't even within 10,000 miles of anything to do with how the exploit actually works.

I've seen the same technique from the attached image in multiple alleged "php2shell exploits", including one on GitHub with over 100 stars. Problem is, it's not php2shell, nor is it even a vulnerability at all. It's a technique known as "session poisoning", which can be leveraged to exploit local file inclusion (LFI) vulnerabilities in PHP apps (not PHP itself).

The only thing it has in common with CVE-2026-109618/CVE-2026-109619 is they both use the "PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" feature. And mitigation advice for both issues reference setting "session.upload_progress.enabled" to "Off".

People are shoving loose details of the vulnerability into LLMs, the LLMs are keying in on the "PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" string, then generating session poisoning code that has nothing to do with the actual CVE. And because the people doing this have absolutely no idea what they're doing, they're confident enough to post their "proof of concept exploit" to GitHub and share it on social media.

So if you see people talking about "session poisoning + LFI" it's likely their LLM hallucinated an exploit based on a 2018 blog by Orange Tsai talking about a local file inclusion attack vector.

What's even worse is that "security researchers" are then using LLMs to triage these exploitation attempts, falling victim to the same hallucinations, then confirming there is ongoing mass-exploitation (there currently isn't).

The actual real exploit is very difficult to exploit, and so far I've not seen anyone successfully get it working on more than a handful of PHP version with highly-specific configurations.

LLMs are useful tools in the hands of skilled professionals, but for others, they're often just a Dunning-Kruger accelerator.

Php2shell Needs a Shell

🚨 This time the bug isn’t in your code, it’s in PHP itself.

PHP2Shell is two CVEs in the PHP runtime (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) that can lead to unauthenticated RCE.

When something like this lands, the first question is usually: what exactly is affected, and what do I need to patch?

I’d rather answer that from the terminal than from twelve browser tabs.

With the ZEN SecDB CLI:

1️⃣ secdb search php2shell

finds both CVEs.

2️⃣ secdb cve CVE-2026-109618

gives the full record: description, CVSS 4.0 at 9.2, CVSS 3.1 at 9.8, vectors, references and vendor advisories from Debian, Red Hat, SUSE, Ubuntu, Arch, Gentoo, FreeBSD and others.

That’s useful because you can quickly check whether your distro already ships a fix, instead of going through each security tracker manually.

If you run PHP, upgrade to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or use the patched package provided by your distro.

Configuration mitigations may reduce the risk, but they don’t replace patching.

And if the server was exposed, it’s probably worth checking whether it was already compromised.

Everyone covered the PHP2Shell CVSS score and the emergency patch on 21 October. The line worth reading sits under that.

The same two bugs (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) hit every server running PHP. What split the outcomes was not patching speed on the day. It was set weeks earlier: whether there was an asset inventory, whether the runtime was still supported, whether there was a WAF whose rules could be changed, whether the update path had been tested.

The teams running one command had those. The teams deciding whether to pull servers offline did not. A critical flaw with a same-day patch mostly tests preparation that already existed, or did not.

PHP2Shell field report — the attacker-side view.

The first exploit-shaped request hit our Mirage honeypot fleet at 21:57 UTC on 20 Oct, ~16h before the patch embargo lifted. Over the next 48h: 9 source IPs, 7 countries, 2 distinct attack shapes.

Highlights:

One actor swept body size <1KB → 16KB+, 200+ unique payloads in 2 min — live calibration of the OOM trigger
The lead tool stamps ----p2shell<hex> into its multipart boundary: a zero-false-positive detection tell we haven’t seen documented elsewhere
A B8RAT/1.0 actor reaching for the deserialization path (CVE-2026-109619) while others hammer the OOM path (CVE-2026-109618)
Independent confirmation of the pre-disclosure exploitation Amazon & Cloudflare reported, from a second sensor network

Full writeup + IOCs:

MISP's galaxy matrix statistics view (app/View/Users/statistics_galaxymatrix.ctp) renders the galaxy name directly into HTML output via sprintf() without any HTML encoding. An authenticated user holding the perm_galaxy_editor permission can create or modify a galaxy whose name contains arbitrary HTML or JavaScript markup. Because the value is interpolated verbatim into the page, any user who subsequently opens the galaxy matrix statistics page will have the embedded script executed in their browser context. This enables session hijacking, credential theft, data exfiltration, or the performance of arbitrary actions on behalf of the victim within the MISP application.

Version affected: <2.5.47

posts.content: CVE-2026-47321: CompressionFilter inflates incoming data with no size limit, so a high-ratio zip bomb can exhaust app memory (DoS). CVSS 7.5, no patch yet. Apply a size limit or restrict untrusted input now. #CVE #infosec #cybersecurity https://www.valtersit.com/cve/CVE-2026-47321/

CVE-2026-47321.description:
The CompressionFilter class uses ZLib to deflate and inflate data sent and received. When we inflate incoming data, the filter does not control the resulting size, and create a buffer no matter what.

Some compressed data may have a compression ration greater than 1 thousand, leading to an exhaustion of the application memory, as we don't control the deflated size.




The fix adds such a control by allowing the application developer to provide a fixed size limit, which when reached throws an exception. It also allows the user to provide a compression ratio that should not be exceeded, protected the application from small inflated files that inflate in gigantic files, but with a grace limit for the resulting size (1Mb) to avoid false positive (like a very small file inflating with a high ratio, but resulting with a acceptable size, like a few thousands bytes)




For application using this feature, it is highly recommended to create the CompressionFilter and to pass the maximum limit as a forth constructor parameter, maxDecompressedSize:




public CompressionFilter(final boolean compressInbound, final boolean compressOutbound, final int compressionLevel, final int maxDecompressedSize)Optionally one can also provide a maxDecompressRatio fifth parameter, and a decompressRatioMinSize sixth parameter to allow small inflated files with a high compression ratio to still be accepted.




Here are the additional constructor:






public CompressionFilter(final boolean compressInbound, final boolean compressOutbound,



            final int compressionLevel, final int maxDecompressedSize,



            final long maxDecompressRatio, final long decompressRatioMinSize)








Also note that a fluent API has been added to spare the users the pain to call a constructor with that many parameters:






 CompressionFilter compressionFilter = new CompressionFilter()

                                                .setCompressionLevel(Zlib.COMPRESSION_MAX)

                                                .setMaxDecompressedSize(1_000_000)

                                                .setMaxDecompressRatio(100).

                                                .setDecompressRatioMinSize(100_000); 









Applications using Apache MINA are advised to upgrade and configure their CompressionFilter instance.

Patch to 2.12.1+ and restrict user permissions. https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-54630-cwe-434-unrestricted-upload-of-file-with-dangerous-type-in-part-db-part-db-server-3e3f77096f8d900f #OffSeq #CVE #RCE #infosec

CVE-2026-54630.description: Part-DB is an open source inventory management system for electronic components. Prior to version 2.12.1, the part attachment upload handler stores uploaded files under the web-served media directory using the client-supplied file extension, and its extension blocklist does not include phar. AttachmentSubmitHandler::renameBlacklistedExtensions() rewrites dangerous extensions (php, phtml, sh, cgi, py, js, html, htaccess, ...) to .txt, but phar is absent from the list, so a .phar file keeps its extension. Public attachments (the default) are written into public/media/, which is the Apache document root. The shipped Apache configuration routes .phar to PHP-FPM, so the stored file is executed as PHP on request. The per-attachment-type extension filter is empty by default and is not consulted by the upload handler in a way that blocks this, and a non-admin user in the default users group can create an attachment type with no filter and attach files to parts. Any authenticated user in the default users group uploads a .phar attachment to a part and fetches it under /media/, executing arbitrary PHP as the www-data web user. Ability to exploit depends on the webserver config, docker image contained the vulnerability by default. This issue has been patched in version 2.12.1.

CVE-2026-94215.description: A flaw was found in the Admin REST API of Keycloak, an open-source identity and access management solution. The issue occurs because the API uses a per-request in-memory cache to resolve clients by their unique identifier without verifying if the client belongs to the realm specified in the request path. This allows an administrator with limited privileges to read or modify sensitive client configurations in the master realm by accessing them through a realm they control. Successful exploitation could lead to the exposure of client credentials or the redirection of administrative login attempts to malicious sites.

The issue occurs when an administrator enforces a stronger authentication flow, such as mandatory two-factor authentication (2FA) setup, through a client policy. A user can bypass this requirement by manually visiting a specific session restart web link during the login process. This action clears the internal markers that track the required security steps, allowing the user to log in with only a password and gain access without completing the mandated 2FA setup.

CVE-2026-93479.description:
A vulnerability exists in NGINX Plus and NGINX Open Source when a map directive uses regex matching and the root directive or access log format references the map's regex capture variables before referencing the map output variable. Alternatively, the same result could be achieved by using a non-cacheable variable in a string expression under certain conditions. An unauthenticated attacker along with conditions beyond their control can exploit this vulnerability by sending crafted HTTP requests. This may cause a heap buffer overflow in the NGINX worker process leading to a restart. Additionally, attackers can execute code on systems with Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) disabled or when the attacker can bypass ASLR.

Impact: 
This vulnerability may allow remote attackers to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) on the NGINX system or to possibly trigger a code execution. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.

Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.

posts.content:
Security Advisory: CVE-2025-71438 - Out-of-Bounds Read in GPAC/MP4Box

Processing a crafted AC-4 stream with an invalid `frame_rate_index` triggers an out-of-bounds read in `gf_odf_ac4_cfg_dsi_v1`, causing MP4Box to crash.

Summary:
The `gf_odf_ac4_cfg_dsi_v1` function in `odf/descriptors.c` uses a stream-supplied `frame_rate_index` to index into fixed-size lookup tables (`AC4_SAMPLE_DELTA_TABLE_48`, `AC4_MEDIA_TIMESCALE_48`). The function does not validate that the index is within bounds before performing the table lookup. A crafted AC-4 file carrying an out-of-range index (e.g., 15) causes an out-of-bounds read, ultimately resulting in a NULL dereference and process crash.

CWE:
CWE-125 - Out-of-bounds Read

Affected Component:
```
odf/descriptors.c:2179
Function: gf_odf_ac4_cfg_dsi_v1()
```

Affected Product:
MP4Box (GPAC Multimedia Open Source Project)

Affected Version:
2.5-DEV-rev1617-g856674b22-master; commit `856674b226d6cbe28a941ad223be38194cbf7d37`. Any codebase equivalent to this commit that has not applied the fix commit is affected.

Attack Conditions:
An attacker supplies a specially crafted AC-4 stream file containing an invalid `frame_rate_index` value. Local access is required; the victim must invoke `MP4Box -dash 100 <crafted_file>` or any equivalent DASH segmentation command that triggers the AC-4 configuration descriptor parsing path.

Impact:
The out-of-bounds read leads to an immediate process crash (SEGV READ at address 0x000000000000), resulting in Denial of Service. No evidence of arbitrary code execution was observed.

Fix / mitigation status:
The issue was fixed in GPAC commit:
```
13eb5b76560aaf7813b865a2ad433258478e2695
```
Users should update to a GPAC build containing this commit or later.

References:

- Issue: https://github.com/gpac/gpac/issues/3303
- PoC: https://github.com/sigdevel/pocs/blob/main/res/gpac/MP4Box/50/50_gf_odf_ac4_cfg_dsi_v1_odf_descriptors_c_2179
- Fix: https://github.com/gpac/gpac/commit/13eb5b76560aaf7813b865a2ad433258478e2695

Credit
Alexander A. Shvedov (@sigdevel)

#fuzzing #infosec #security #afl++ #revers #cybersecurity #bugbounty #vulnerability #opensource #linux #cve #advisory #gpac

posts.content:
@lienrag @mgorny Normally, when you use pip to install packages, it installs the latest versions that satisfies “the given constraints”. These certainly include constraints given on the command line; whether this also includes dependency metadata of packages already installed inside the venv in use, I'm not sure (would have to check).

Anyway, there are circumstances in which developers want to have an easy way to install a set of packages with clearly defined versions (to have things reproducible, especially when the venv creation is automated). This is what lock files do: they record the versions of the packages you want to “pin” (normally, compatible versions!). Of course, you need to update the lock file when there is a security update for one of the locked packages, or it will be blocked...

The link given earlier by @mgorny is full of expert advice. If you don't want to micro-manage your venvs, I believe the following should be safe:

  1. Make sure your distro has patched everything related to these problems (in particular, that the distro-shipped pip doesn't use the compromised CA certificates).

  2. Delete your existing venvs (I assume they contain no interesting data, only installed packages).

  3. Recreate them in a way that does not force vulnerable versions to be installed: should be fine unless you use lock files or otherwise hardcode version requirements.

For me, the hardest part was 1: for instance, one can see in the pip ChangeLog that upstream pip ugraded its bundled certifi package, however the ChangeLog entry does not mention any CVE, therefore checking whether my distro-provided pip is safe was difficult, until the very recent 26.2.2+dfsg-1 changelog.Debian.gz entry for python3-pip clarified things:

python-pip (26.2.2+dfsg-1) unstable; urgency=high

  * New upstream release.
    - Note that while this version contains a critical certifi security update
      upstream, for Debian this is completely delegated to ca-certificates.
    - CVE-2026-13346: Correctly handle handle doubly-encoded package URLs
      (Closes: #1143072)
  * Refresh patches.
  * Update copyright.

 -- Stefano Rivera <ste...an.org>  Wed, 21 Oct 2026 16:04:45 +0200

(this just reached unstable a few minutes ago).

CVE-2026-13346.description:
pip would incorrectly handle doubly-encoded package URLs from indexes allowing for files to be installed to arbitrary locations on disk even when installing wheels.

This vulnerability requires downloading or installing a package from a malicious package index to succeed, malicious packages alone are not able to exploit this vulnerability. Note that this vulnerability only materially impacts users running `pip download` with the `--only-binary` option as installing source distributions from an untrusted index is already an unsafe operation that executes code during install time.

CVE-2026-105944.description:
Apache Pulsar Manager is a web console for administering Apache Pulsar clusters. It has its own user accounts and login, and it can be configured with an HTTP authentication credential, such as a token, that it uses to call the Pulsar admin API on behalf of its users. Pulsar Manager has the following security issues:

- The operation for creating the initial administrator (superuser) account is available without authentication, and it remains available after the instance has been initialized. Anyone who can reach Pulsar Manager can create an additional administrator account at any time and log in with it. This issue affects versions 0.3.0 and later.
- Requests to the Pulsar admin API that Pulsar Manager proxies to the configured Pulsar cluster are not subject to Pulsar Manager's authentication. Version 0.2.0 checks the caller's permissions for some of these requests, but not for all of them. An unauthenticated user can therefore use Pulsar Manager to send requests to the Pulsar admin API, which the cluster processes with the credential configured in Pulsar Manager.
- The destination of a proxied request can be chosen by the requester, and Pulsar Manager attaches its configured Pulsar admin credential to the request. An unauthenticated user can make Pulsar Manager send this credential to a host of the user's choosing, and the credential can then be used directly against the Pulsar cluster.
- In versions 0.3.0 and later, Pulsar Manager does not distinguish between privilege levels of its accounts. Every account, including one created through the first issue, effectively has full administrative privileges in Pulsar Manager.

The impact depends on the version and the deployment. In versions 0.3.0 and later, any user who can reach Pulsar Manager over the network can take full control of Pulsar Manager. In all versions, when Pulsar Manager is configured with an HTTP authentication credential for a Pulsar cluster, any user who can reach Pulsar Manager can perform the Pulsar admin operations that this credential permits and can obtain the credential itself. When Pulsar Manager is configured with the token signing key of a Pulsar cluster, an administrator of Pulsar Manager can create tokens for the cluster.

Apache Pulsar Manager is no longer maintained and is completely unsupported. The Apache Pulsar PMC has retired it. There are no supported versions, and no further releases, fixes or security updates will be made for any version. These issues will not be fixed.

Using Pulsar Manager is not recommended. Users should stop using Pulsar Manager, remove existing deployments, and move to one of the alternatives described in the Administration UI documentation (https://pulsar.apache.org/docs/administration-ui). Users who have exposed Pulsar Manager configured with a Pulsar credential or token signing key should also consider replacing that credential or key.

Until a deployment is removed, users should not expose Pulsar Manager to untrusted networks, and should restrict network access to it to trusted administrators.

CVE-2026-105869.description:
Apache Pulsar's MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider authorizes a client with all roles listed in a claim of its JSON Web Token (JWT). The provider is intended for use with token authentication, which verifies the token before authorization. The provider did not verify the token itself: it parsed the token's claims with the signature removed and trusted that authentication had already checked it.

When authentication and authorization are enabled with a non-empty anonymousUserRole setting, some HTTP requests whose credentials fail authentication are not rejected, but are handled as requests of the anonymous user role. For the broker's HTTP endpoints, such as the admin REST API, this fallback applies to requests that do not name an authentication method and requires strictAuthMethod to be false (the default) where that setting is available. For the WebSocket API, failed credentials can also fall back to the anonymous user role; this path does not enforce strictAuthMethod. The authentication data kept for such a request still contained the request's Authorization header. MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider then read the bearer token from that header without verifying its signature and authorized the request with the roles in the token's role claim.

As a result, in deployments that use MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider together with a non-empty anonymousUserRole and that permit this fallback, an unauthenticated client can send an HTTP request, for example to the admin REST API or the WebSocket API, with a forged or unsigned token that lists arbitrary roles, and be authorized with those roles. The impact can include super-user access when the token lists a role configured in superUserRoles, allowing the client to read and change tenants, namespaces, topics, permissions and broker configuration. No valid credentials are required.

Deployments are not affected if they use the default authorization provider (PulsarAuthorizationProvider) or another authorization provider, or if anonymousUserRole is not set (the default). Requests that authenticate successfully with a valid token are not affected, because the token that MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider reads is the token that authentication verified. Connections that use the Pulsar binary protocol are not affected by this issue, because the broker does not keep client authentication data for connections that it assigns to the anonymous user role.

In fixed versions, MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider obtains roles only from tokens that the configured token authentication provider has verified, using its configured keys and validation settings. Broker HTTP requests that are assigned to the anonymous user role are authorized only as that role, and invalid tokens cannot supply additional roles to WebSocket requests. The broker fails to start if MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider is configured with authorization enabled but without a token authentication provider.

This issue affects Apache Pulsar versions from 2.8.1 before 4.0.14 and from 4.1.0 before 4.2.5.

- 4.0.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.0.14.
- 4.1.x and 4.2.x version users should upgrade to at least 4.2.5.

Users operating versions prior to those listed above should upgrade to the aforementioned patched versions or newer versions.

The currently supported Apache Pulsar release lines are 4.0.x and 5.0.x. The supported versions schedule is available at https://pulsar.apache.org/contribute/release-policy/.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately can remove the anonymousUserRole setting from the broker and WebSocket service configurations, or restrict network access to the HTTP endpoints of these services to trusted clients.

CVE-2025-15467.description:
Issue summary: Parsing CMS AuthEnvelopedData or EnvelopedData message with
maliciously crafted AEAD parameters can trigger a stack buffer overflow.

Impact summary: A stack buffer overflow may lead to a crash, causing Denial
of Service, or potentially remote code execution.

When parsing CMS (Auth)EnvelopedData structures that use AEAD ciphers such as
AES-GCM, the IV (Initialization Vector) encoded in the ASN.1 parameters is
copied into a fixed-size stack buffer without verifying that its length fits
the destination. An attacker can supply a crafted CMS message with an
oversized IV, causing a stack-based out-of-bounds write before any
authentication or tag verification occurs.

Applications and services that parse untrusted CMS or PKCS#7 content using
AEAD ciphers (e.g., S/MIME (Auth)EnvelopedData with AES-GCM) are vulnerable.
Because the overflow occurs prior to authentication, no valid key material
is required to trigger it. While exploitability to remote code execution
depends on platform and toolchain mitigations, the stack-based write
primitive represents a severe risk.

The FIPS modules in 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, 3.3 and 3.0 are not affected by this
issue, as the CMS implementation is outside the OpenSSL FIPS module
boundary.

OpenSSL 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, 3.3 and 3.0 are vulnerable to this issue.

OpenSSL 1.1.1 and 1.0.2 are not affected by this issue.

CVE-2026-56388.description:
The Redis server command parser in Apache bRPC accepts an empty RESP array as a command header. A remote unauthenticated attacker who can reach a bRPC server with Redis service enabled can send an empty array header followed by a bulk string, causing an out-of-bounds write in the parser and crashing the process.

Root Cause:
RedisCommandParser::ConsumeImpl rejected negative RESP array counts but accepted zero. It resized the command argument vector to zero elements and continued parsing. When a following bulk string was parsed, the only index guard was a CHECK. In configurations where fatal logs do not abort immediately, execution could continue and write to _args[0] even though the vector was empty.

Affected Scenarios:
Deployments that enable ServerOptions.redis_service and accept Redis protocol traffic from untrusted clients. The issue is reached during parsing before command handling or authentication.

How to Fix:
1. Upgrade bRPC to version 1.18.0, which fixes this issue.
2. Apply this patch:  https://github.com/apache/brpc/pull/3354 

Note:
The fix rejects empty RESP arrays as invalid Redis commands and replaces the internal index CHECK with an explicit parse error so malformed command streams cannot fall through to an indexed vector write.

CVE-2026-80521.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

af_unix: Unlink scc_entry in unix_del_edge().

Kyle Zeng reported that GC could free a dead SCC partially.

The scenario is as follows:

   1) Create two SCCs:

       X -.   A <-> B
       ^--'

   2) Run the following concurrently:

      2-1) send() sk-B to sk-B from sk-X
      2-2) close() both A and B

At 2-1), there is a small window where unix_add_edges()
publishes a new edge (B <-> B) to GC but its skb is not queued
by skb_queue_tail().

If 2-2) completes before skb_queue_tail() and GC is triggered,
it judges A <-> B as dead, but B is not freed because GC cannot
collect the not-yet-queued skb holding the B <-> B edge.

       X -.   A <-> B -. This edge is visible
       ^--'         ^..'  but skb is not

This itself is not a problem since the next GC run will judge
B as dead as well and free it finally.

       X -.   A <.> B -.
       ^--'         ^--'

However, X's SCC forces the next GC to call unix_walk_scc_fast(),
and it iterates over A through B's scc_entry.

Let's unlink scc_entry before freeing the vertex in unix_del_edge().

CVE-2026-15723.description: GitLab has remediated an issue in GitLab CE/EE affecting all versions from 10.1 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1 that, when OmniAuth SAML and LDAP auto-linking were both enabled, an authenticated user could have taken over an existing LDAP-backed account without any interaction from the targeted user, due to improper input sanitization in the LDAP email lookup path used during OmniAuth identity linking.
